From the Weekly Courier and New Fork Enquirer, June 8, 1839. The whig press in England, denounce the conduct of Sir Ron hut Peel, and appear to have succeeded in enlisting the popular feeling to a very considerable extent, in favour of the stand taken by the Queen. Her sex, her youth, and the delicacy of the point in dispute, render this not unnatural. Yet perhaps, the truth is, that the Tory party were not willing to enter oflice without the means of retaining it permanently and of exercising a commanding influence over the direction of many important events, which may speedily be expected to take place. Such for instance, as the selection of the future husband of the Queen. It is but in the ordinary course of things, that those immediately surrounding her should have an important influence in deciding her choice, and that as her court is at present constituted, this choice would be adverse from the views of the Tory party, and perhaps preclude them for a long time, from the chance of regaining the direction of the politics of England. Riots continued to break out in many parts of England and Wales, instigated oy the Chartists ; but as they are not of an alarming character, and are speedily put down hy the veoinanary cavalry of the counties where tliey occur, with the assistance of a few regulars, we make no extracts concerning them. The position of the monicd market and commercial affairs in England still appear to us such as to render gieat prudence necessary in those here who are liable to he alluded hy it. Great commercial distress still pervades
many of the provincial towns in Fiance. M.

London, May 1 h, 1839. Parliament has been prorogued until the 27th mst., and it is understood that important changes in the Cabinet arc then to he announced. The English radicals who voted against the government on the Jamaica . ' hill, have made a proposition lor continuing their support to the Wing administration, which is that certain progressive measures shall he taken up in consonance with the general national feeling, in favor of a more rapid leibrm that has lately been diseernable in the conduct of the Whigs. Lord John Kussel, who has distinguished himself as the opponent ot further measures ol reform, it is thought will now be compelled to retire, and probably a more liberal policy on the questions of the ballot and the Corn Laws, may now he expected to be promised by the Whigs. The speaker of the House of Commons has resigned in consequence of his health and on the reassembling of Parliament a great tiia! of strength is to take place between the factions, on the appointment of the new speaker. Mr. Goulbourn being the canditate put lorwurd hy the Tories, and Mr. Shaw Le Fevre being the O government candidate for the chair. O The Whigs, however, are tolerably sure of success, and of continuing in power for some time to come, as though the English radicals

þÿ as Sir W. Moles worth, Mr. Hume, Mr. Grote, and others who voted against them on the Jamaica hill, are too honorable to be the tools of any party whatsoever þÿ yet on the other hand. Mr O'Connell, who can effectually turn the scale in following the Whigs through thick and thin, for this man is very evidently weary of poverty and agitation, and is very generally expected to seize upon the first offer which presents itself of a post of sufficient importance to make the fortunes of himself and his several almost pennyless sons. Such is the state of affairs so far as the several factions are arrayed at the present time. On the other hand, the party of the Chartists, or in other words, the millions of the working population of the country, are also in considerable commotion, and the subject of considerable alarm. The petition embodying the principles of the " People's Charter," has been signed by 1,250,000 persons, and is to he presented to the House of Commons, by Mr. Thomas Attwood, on an early day after the recess. The leaders of the Chartist party have lately gone down to Birmingham to agitate that and the neighboring districts þÿ and there are reports that vast bodies of the people are possessed of arms, and that the country is on the verge of political movements of no ordinary kind. The government has not as yet done more than arrest one or two of the leading members of the Convention, and taken measures for concentrating great bodies of troops and a strong force of artillery around Birming-

ham and the principal manufacturing towns; and >t is believed that the petition will he received hy the House of Commons, and a soothing conduct ho pursued on the occasion -of its presentation. Altogether the political condition of England is one of unusual interest at the present time. Lest the letter of your Paris correspondent should chance þÿ as on the last occasion of the

sailing of the Great Western, to arrive too late þÿ I briefly notice tlie occurrence of another insurrection in Paris, on Sunday last, accompanied by the former method of fighting by barricades, but which were all carried by the troops and the insurrection suppressed, with the loss of.about 150 lives, of which 50 were of the regular troops and the National Guards. In the midst of the terror which this movement created at the Tuilleries, an administration was at length formed with Marshal Soult at its head þÿ to the total exclusion of Mons. Thiers þÿ who could not even secure for himself the presidency of the Chamber of Deputies, having been outvoted by a majority of 9. These events have greatly strengthened the position of the King. The English money market is very dull in all its departments, and money has been gradually becoming more valuable for several days past. The Bank of England at the weekly court of the directors held yesterday afternoon, advanced the rate of interest to 5 per cent. þÿ a measure to which they would not have resorted were not the bullion in their vaults reduced to a very limited amount. London, May 15. Lord Melbourne rose for the purpose of making the ' Ministerial explanations.' It will be seen that his Lordship fully corroborated the statement of Sir It. Peel, but was as careful as Lord John Russell had been to avoid explaining what the misunderstanding about the ladies of the household could possibly have to do with the ground on which he

and his colleagues resigned. He told the house that the Queen had labored under the impression (which he admitted to be an errw neous one) that Sir It. Peel intended to remove all the ladies of the bedchamber, as well as some of those who filled inferior situations in the household ! He denied that there had been any intrigue in the case, or that the objection as to changing the household had been preconcerted for the purpose of rendering abortive any attempt to form another Administration. He said he did not care about being accused of tenacity of office, but that he did not like to be accused of running away tiom his post (if he always runs back to his post as fast as he did on this occasion, he would outstrip all such accusations,) and that he resumed office only because he would not abandon his Sovereign when demands were made of her with which he thought she ought not to comply ! The Duke of Wellington replied in a most manly and dignified speech, which he will not attempt to describe further than to say that it must carry conviction to the mind of every honest man who reads it. The following passage appears to have made Lord Melbournfeel very uncomfortable as well indeed he might : þÿ " 1 cannot, my Lords," said the noble Duke, " I cannot but think that the principles on which we proposed to act with respect to the ladies of the bedchamber in the case of a Queen regnant were the correct principles. (Hear, hear) The public will not believe that the Queen holds no political conversa-

tions with those ladies (hear, hear,) and that political influence is not exercised by them, particularly considering who those persons are who hold such situations. (Hear, hear.) I believe the history of this country affords a number of instances in which secret and improper influence has been exercised by means of such conversations. I have, my Lords a somewhat strong opinion on this subject. I

The British Queen. þÿ This noble steamer is to sail Irom Portsmouth on the 1st of July . and we are indebted to her consigness, Messrs: Wards worth & Smith, for a plan of her cabin, by which it appears that she will accommodate upwards of two hundred passengers. She registers 2010 tons, and we saw her in the Thames, we were of opinion that she will be admitted, on her arrival here, to be of a beautiful model, decidedly American in its character, and equal to some of those ships which have won for our builders such universal applause throughout the civilized world. She is indeed, a mammoth steamer> and as beautiful as she is large. We are happy to learn that Capt. Roberts who visited us in the Sirius, will command her, jand we congratulate the public upon the certainty of now having more steam communication with England. When the Great Western sailed nearly all the berths in the Biitish Queen had been taken, and it was supposed that she would have a full freight of 800 tons measurement. The following is an extract from a letter from a gentleman in Glasgow : þÿ ' I yesterday went down to see the British Queen. They are completing the ladies cabin, and next week put in old cloths, carpets, beds, and begin to pain! her from stem to stern, outside and in. You will, as will every body else, be surprised at her massive machinery. All round (he engine room there is a wide walk (on a level with die saloon floor) protected by a brass railing, so that visitors and passengers may have a tine view

of the machinery without interfering with the men. There is a separate entrance to it from the deck; the ceiling of it is panelled, and is to be painted oak and varnished They are cutting port holes for putting in coals under deck, and Roberts declares she shall be kept clean. You will be highly gratified with her arrangements throughout. Her "funnel" was lying on deck, and 1 took a promanade of CO feet through, hat on and all standing."

From the St. James's Chronicle, May 28. AFFAIRS OF THE EAST. The war between Turkey and Egypt has taken every one by surprise. The letters from Constantinople and Alexandria, as well as the journals of Turkey and Egypt, were all more or less paeilie. The Smyrna journals have alone cast anv doubt upon the subject, and but little attention has been paid to them. It would seem that the Viceroy himself was the first to have communicated to the European consuls at Alexandria the intelligence which has now reached us, and which has created in the diplomatic world ; sensation it would he quite impossible to describe. þÿ lie I Mediterranean is to be covered with French sails. The orders sent to the ports ol 1 onion and Marseilles hv Admiral Duperrfi have been as prompt as they have been cxiensivc, and the demand for 10 millions of francs made yesterday docs not find a single opponent in the press. The following letter from Alexandria is interesting, not because it

3i3M:g3mro3 AVIS announces the war in direct terms hut be cause it is of such a nature as (o prepare the reader for the events which have followed. þÿ I send you herewith a mass of letters from the East They contain the latest news re ceived in Paris : þÿ þÿ Alexandria, May 8. þÿ I hasten to send vou a copy of the follow intr official document. It is too important to lose time in correcting the style. It is a letter from Artin Hey, the first Secretary of the Viceroy, to Boghos Bey, dated April 28th, front Chibin, in Lower Egypt: þÿ 1 1 is highness the generalissimo (Ibrahim i Pacha) has written to inform the Viceroy that the forces of the Sultan have crossed the frontier at Bilegic (called in our maps Bir, on the Euphrates), where they have erected some fortifications. Ilis highness the generalissimo, after having ordered several regiments cantoned in Syria to march towards Aleppo, is about to proccd thither himself. His highness the Viceroy, having considered it probable that this step of the Sultan lias been taken wilh a view to throw the blame of having made the first show of hostilities upon him, has written to the generalissimo to make no i advance until he is perfectly assured of the progress of the Sultan's troops, hut to put his trust in God, and to act with appropriate energy should the approach of these forces be confirmed in a positive manner. þÿ His highness i fie Viceroy charges vonr Excellency to communicate forthwith to the consuls general of the European powers the information which 1 have had the honor of

transmitting to you. (Signed) þÿ ARTIN BE1V þÿ The Turkish army, consisting of 50,000 men, is well supplied with artillery, and has proceeded to Syria with the hope of ezeiting a general revolt. It is divided into three corps, one of which manoeuvres on the left Bank of the Euphrates, the second has passed the Euphrates at Bir. and the third guards the defiles of the mountains, to render sure the communications and convoys from Constantinople. þÿ The Viceroy has an army of 200,009 men ; of which 100.000 are in Syria, 71,000 infantry and 20.000 cavalry. Ibrahim þÿ1 acha has with him about 30,000 men at the camp lie has formed near Aleppo. The Turkish and Egyptian forces are equally badlv clothed, but on the whole the troops of the Viceroy are superior." The following letter is still more important : þÿ þÿ On board the Leonidas, in the harbour of Syria, on her return from Alexandria, May 10. þÿ War is decidedly declared between the Sultan and Mehemet Ali. Since the 5th no important news had been communicated. þÿ The Pacha has proceeded from Cairo to Damietta. There he receives couriers from Syria, without making known their contents. The corps which forms the left of the Turkish army is in the mountains. That of the right advances towards Bagdad, and will seek to form a junction with the forces of the Pacha ol this place. The ormy is 45.000 strong." The following letter from Alexandria, of the 7th of May, is of no ordinary interest, and tends to confirm the first impression, that
Russia is at the bottom of all this movement : " Alexandria, May 7. þÿ An extraordinary Russian courier arriv. cd on the 5th inst., on hoard the Austrian steam boat, which came direct from Cottslaii

2>&Sr3X tinople. He was the bearer of very interest- j of Saxe Weimar, and nephew of her Majesty ing dispatches for the Count Medem, the Consul General of the empire of Russia. This courier had proceeded from St. Petersburgh to Alexandria in 24 days, and he would not give up his dispatches but to the Russian Consul himself, M. Lavison, w'ho went to the Lazaretto and received them, giving the courier receipt a from the Count Medem. It is also said, that this courier is the bearer of a letter of the greatest importance, written wholly by the Count de Nesselrode, the Minister of Foreign Affairs at St. Petersburg!). þÿ þÿ I will keep you informed as to all that shall transpire relative to thesedispatches. Another letter from Alexandria of the same date says þÿ þÿ The Emperor of Russia has, by his dispatches, ordered the Pacha to withdraw immediately his troops from the frontiers of Syria and to pay the tribute. These demands he cannot comply with. Two Tartars have also arrived at the head quarters of the Pacha ; one, the bearer of an order from the Porte for the tribute; and the other, the hatti sheriff, demanding the execution of the treaty of commerce. Admiral Roussin has been mystified at Constantinople. He wrote but a few days since here, stating that the Turkish troops had received orders to retrogade.

CONSPIRACY AT CONSTANTINE TO MASSACRE THE FRENCH. The French government has received intelligence of the discovery of an extensive and formidable conspiracy to massacre the French in the town and province of Constantine. The chiefs are said to be arrested ; but the general animosity is so great, that unless the French shall quadruple their forces, they will be unable to maintain their ground in that part of the province of Algiers.

From the same, June 1. Paris, May 30. THE AFFAIRS OF HIE EAST. Respecting the great question of war in the East we have no new facts, but abundance of comment and speculation suggested by the discussion in the committees of the Chamber of Deputies yesterday of the demand of 10,000,O00f made by the Minister of Marine for the outlay which it would be necessary to incur in making preparations to meet the circumstances to which that contest might give rise. The committee, it would appear, was composed of the most heterogeneous materials. M. Guizot questioned the gravity which the published accounts attached to the did M. Thiers, who added that þÿ he affair ; as did not believe that Russia had produced the movement of the Turks, nor that England was, as some deputies contended, ready to pounce upon Egypt. All the great Powers dreaded war, while they were each of them disposed to profit by the convulsions of the East. All that could be said of Russia was. that she was the best prepared of any, and the most formidable, and that consequently it was the duty of the Powers of the west of Europe to be upon their guard and ready to throw themselves in the balance.

From the New York Daily Express, Jane 17. CANADIAN MATTERS. The last Montreal and Quebec papers have several interesting items in regard to local movements in the province. It appears that the authorities are busy hunting þÿ þÿrebels, and it would seem not without success. At Montreal on Wednesday the steamer Princess Victoria brought over another rebel named Beausoleil, of the firm of Vallee Sc (Jo. merchants in the New Market street. He was captured on Tuesday at Mis sisquoi Ray, a short distance on this side o' the boundary line, and was armed with a pair of loaded pistols and a dagger. He was one of the most active and influential leaders during the two rebellions, and administered the unlawful oaths to a very great number of the Canadians. One of the Montreal papers says that there is abundance of evidence in possession of the Government to convict him of arson, as he was recognized as the leader on several late occasions when houses were plundered and burned on the frontier. Another rebel named Naysmith, who arrived in town on Friday morning, was lodged in gaol yesterday forenoon, and we understand that the papers found in his possession are of considerable importance. He was disguised in dress and moustached like a hussar, but was soon recognized by the Police, who lodged him in safe quarters. It is reported that several others have also been captured. The Canadian Government, it is understood, intend erecting barracks at Laprairie without delay, þÿ the barracks to be large, and capable of containing about three thousand men. The

building will be of brick, and is to be defended by four strong towers of stone. Most of the brick will be imported from the United States, as the brick fields in Canada could not supply the requisite quantity in time. The loss of the steamer John Hull has created a good deal of excitement in Montreal. The second Engineer and the two sailors of the John Hull, who were missing when that boat was burned, have, it is said, been since seen in Sorel, and that warrants have been

sent down for their a pprehension. It was their watch when the disaster happened, and suspicion of foul play on their part, naturally arises from this circumstance, coupled with their escape unobserved by the other persons present. þÿ Phis is given as a rumour in one of the papers. The melancholy and unprovided situation of the emigrants who were on board the John Hull when she was burned call for immediate and liberal assistance of the inhabitants of Montreal. The feelings of these poor individuals, says the Montreal Courier can neither be imagined or described þÿ strangers in a strange land, without food to eat, raiment to put on, or house to shelter them, they stand alone and starving in the midst of plenty. þÿ The St Paul's lodge of þÿF reemasonshad done something for the relief of these unfortunate individuals. Measures are in progress to reorganize the Militia of Lower Canada.

From the Morning C mirier and New York Enquirer, June 28, 1839. Mackenzie's Trial þÿ We copy from the Rochester Democrat the subjoined report of the defence made by Mackenzie on bis trial. It. is much to be regretted that in such a ea e as the present, we have not some distant spot, þÿ such as Botany Bay or New South Wales, to which convicted criminals of his þÿ description could be transported, for in the sentence now passed on him, we fear the snake is scarcely scotched. Mr. Mackenzie called Dr. James Hunter, who is a freeholder of Upper Canada, and well acquainted with the province. Defendant. Do you know the province of Upper Canada to be a province of the Crown of England ? Mr. Benton. I object to that question. Mr. Mackenzie sustained the propriety of the question. The ownership of Canada by the Crown is an asserted fact in the indictment, and every thing depends upon that presumption. If 1 can prove that Canada is not a province of the Crown, then everv count in the indictment falls. This 1 can do, as verily believe ; and as the question has been permitted by the Court already, I suppose that there can be no objection to its being put now. Mr. Benton. It is enough for this Court to know that Canada is recognized by this Government as a province of the Crown. It is a judicial luct which cannot he controverted.

The Court, therefore, decide that the question is now irrevelnnt. Mr. Mackenzie. May I ask a question relative to tho condition ol the provinces at the time of the outbreak ? The Court. In cutting a ditch across a meadow at Laesten, near Viboig in Jutland, a labourer found in a very watery hog a consideiable collection of Amber Articles, which had been enclosed in a wooden vessel, whereof however only a lew fragments remained. The collection consists of 25 pieces not perforated, but having an identure round the middle, so as that they could be bound last ; 5U0 larger and smaller pieces without any other workmanship than simply their being perforated ; further, 1 hammer shaped and 59 primshaped pieces, 4i>0 cyiindi icol-sbaped beads, and 2850 small round beads, also 50 oblong pieces perforated with 4 or 5 holes, which have served as middle pieces in a necklace of several rows of beads, and 5 end pieces to the same. 4 lie whole quantity, therefore consists of 3900 pieces, weighing 19lb., and | is tiie largest discovery of amber articles known to have been made. About the same time there was received from the Island of Mben several amber articles of precisely the same sori, which were found in a subterraneous chamber, constructed of large granite stones in the lower pai l of a barrow, which were also deposited articles of flint and bone, and several unburned bodies, but nothing whatever ol metal. In the highest part of the same barrow, quite separated from the lower chamber, was a small stone coffin, wherein was found an urn full of burned bones, above which lay several cutting instruments of bronze, such as knives, pincers etc.

'1 ms upper chamber, accordingly, belongs to the biouze peuod, but the lower one, in which me amber articles lay, belongs to the most remote period, or the stone age as it is cauetl. This last discovery serves, like many others, to convince us, that the large discovery ol amber articles now under conside" ration belongs to same period, an inference which is corioborated by the rough work- ; manship of die articles, executed without the help of þÿturner slailie or borer. It is thus evident that we have here obtained the rich | stock of one of the amberdealers of remote I i antiquity. COMMUNICATION WITH INDIA. By the arrangements which will take effect under the convention, the Indian mails will be entirely disconnected from the line of Lisbon and Gibralter steamers. The mails outwards will be carried in sealed boxes and under the charge of an English messenger to Marseilles, whence an English steamer in waiting will convey them to Malta, and Irom thence thev will be forwarded without delay to Alexandria, and overland to the Red Sea and their destination. As regards the homeward mails, the steamer will be in waiting at | Alexandria þÿ on the arrival of the mails she will proceed with the letters forthwith to Alalia þÿ at Malta a ehange of steamers will take place, for the purpose of avoiding some difficulties as to quarantine, and the mails will ire forwarded again by a steamer to Marseilles, where an English messenger will he in waiting, and convev them in his custody and in sealed boxes to Calais By this arrangement we trust that the difficulties and delays which have been complained of will be obviated, and the quickest transmission both of gov eminent communications and private letters secured. The convention is to take effect two months from the ratification of the treaty. By this arrangement the steam communication with India will he placed upon a satisfactory footing, and a rapid communication secured with one of our most important colonial possessions. A contract has already been entered into for a communication by steam with Halifax every fortnight, which

will come into effect in the course of next summer. A similar plan f<>r communication with the VVv st Indies, Mexico and Chargres is now under the consideration of the government with every prospect of success. þÿ Ministerial Paper.

St. Croix Christian step (Monday) 29th July, 1839. On Wednesday night of the last week, a most diabolical attempt was perpetrated in this town on the person of Mr. Mills ( partner of D. Mac Neilledge dp Co). The dwelling of Mr: Mills was entered by some, prowling villain between the hours of 1 1 and 12. Mr: Mills had retired to his bed at the usual hour , and was sound asleep, when he was suddenly awakened In/ the feeling of a powerful man's hand grasping tightly his throat, at the same time several severe stubs were injlicted on his body. Mr: Mills after hard struggling succeeded in relieving himself from the grasp of the murderer, and raised the cry of " Murder" in a loud voice. This cry reached his neighbors, and the midnight assassin, alarmed for his safety, immediately retreated, followed by Mr: Mills who from loss of blood was not able to stop him. Medical aid was instantly procured, and we are happy to learn that the wounds of Mr: Mills although severe, are not considered da t'gerous. An occurrence of so horrible a nature in our quiet and orderly community is we believe, not in the recollection of the oldest inhabitant. þÿ Every effort is making by the Police to discover <$ convict the perpetrator and it is to lie hoped, for the. safety of the community, that these efforts will be, successful.

We arc indebted to the Salopian Journal received this morning, for tiie following admirable letter from tbc Duke of Wellington, forwarded to Sir liichard Jenkins, M. P , and addressed to the inhabitants of the town and neighbourhood of Shrewsbury who signed the loval þÿdeclaration, which appearedt with Sir li. þÿPeel answer, s in the St. James's Chronicle of Thursday last þÿ Tilfci I>UlvK Of þÿWELLINGTON S LETTER. (From the Salopian Journal ) þÿ London June 5, 1839. þÿ 1 tun much flattered and gratified by the opinion of the gentlemen of Shrewsbury and the neighbourhood, that my right hon. iriend Sir Robert Peel and I have not conducted ourselves towards our Sovereign with disloyal insolence. My first impression on the calumnies which you have noticed were, as those of the gentlemen of Shrewsbury, those of contempt as well for the calumnies themselves as for the persons of those with whom they originated, and of those who circulated them.

3&A1T3Z 'TJ83T-JW3>-I3'Z þÿ3f8SUTh rT©3AT33» þÿ The ministers of the Sovereign thought proper to resign their ollices, very much to mv astonishment. þÿ 1 was called upon, and then my right honourable friend, Sir Robert Peel, to undertake the direction of the affairs of our Soþÿvereign s government. He undertook the charge, and I was willing to serve in any way that might he wished, in or out of office, in any otlice, or without emolument or patronage. þÿ I had no proposition to submit to the Sovereign, and submitted none. But 1 concurred in those by my right hon. friend Sir Robert Peel. I thought that they were founded on the principle on which all preceding ad ministration had been formed ; on that alone on which the affairs of the state can he conducted with honour to those concerned in conducting them, þÿ with satisfaction, and even with security to the Sovereign. þÿ YY?e have heard much at different times of the exercise and power of secret influence in the Palace, probably more than was consistent with truth on the occasions on which such influence was complained oi. But it never was pretended at any period that such influence was not prejudicial to the conduct of public alfairs. I had upon a former occasion felt the inconvenience of an anomalous influ enee of this description, and 1 was the more anxious to avoid now to expose myself and the public service to the risk of suffering from the real or even supposed exercise of such an influence þÿ The consequence of the propositions of my right hon. friend, made with mv con-

currence was, that the arrangement of an administration as suggested could not he made ; and the ministers who had resigned resumed their several offices. þÿ The affair would there have terminated if it had not been deemed expedient to charge my right honourable friend and myself with insolence þÿ disloyal insolence þÿ to our Movereign, and to raise a cry against us on tliat ground However, I may regret that these transactions should become the subject of discussion, I cannot be surprised that gentlemen of honor and character, such as those resident in and in the neighbourhood of Shrewsbury who have signed this declaration, should he anxious to declare that they do not concur in the address voted in that town ; that they consider to be calumnious the imputation ol disloyal insolence against public men whose only faults were their readiness to serve their Sovereign when their services were called for, notwithstanding the difficulties ol the times, and that they submitted to the Sovereign propositions founded on the known principles of the constiution. þÿ In proportion as the gentlemen who have signed this declaration teel contempt for the calumnies which the address contains, and for those who have thus recognised, recorded, and propagated them, must they feel anxious to record by their declaration their dissent from them, þÿ It is very satisfactory to me to receive this declaration from a gentleman who is the representative in the House of Commons of the town of Shrewsbury, for Whom, on ac-
count ol former recollections and services, as well as on account of the station he tills, his acquirements and reputation, 1 must ever led the highest respect. þÿWELLINGTON.

Treasures of the West. þÿ The Buffalo Commercial Advertiser announces, under its marine head, the arrival at that port, of the ship Milwaukie, Capt. Dickson, from St. Joseph's with nine thousand bushels wheat and eight hundred barrels flour. This is but a loretaste of the riches of the bountiful and boundless West. That vast granary is just beginning to unfould itself. That fertile soil has but just yielded itself to the harrow and the cradle. From the, Saratoga Exchange,- Mournful Casuamiy. þÿ We are informed that a child aged about 10 years, the daughter of Mr. Abraham Welch, who resides about ten miles in the forest, North of Lake Pleasant, was torn in pieces, and almost entirely devoured, by panther a of the largest size, on Monday week. The child was playingonthe bank of a small stream, within sight and hearing of the house, when the panther sprang from a thicket of hemlock, and seized her by the neck, and after dragging her into the thicket, proceeded to devour her at leisure. The mother of the littie girl had gone to a spring a few rods below the

The Eng- i house, for the purpose of obtaining a pail of water, and she returned just in time to sec the monster leap the creek with the last remaining limb of her daughter hanging from his mouth. Mrs. Welch comprehended at a glance the extent of the calamity, and she immediately ran for her husband, who was engaged in making shingles, nearly a mile and a half in the woods from the house. He immediately started in pursuit of the ferocious animal but did not succed in capturing bint. All that could be lound ol the little sufferer was part of her frock, and some hair, J all clotted and matted in blood.

Mr. B. however, succeeded in freeing himself from his grasp, and again brougnt Inin manfully to the suilace, where lie most fortunately derived temporary rebel from a plank, winch tiad been thrown out from the steamboat, and enabled him to sustain Ins burthen j until he coulil reach a boat belonging to a schooner lying at the wharf, which he had just

Koefoed having received an official appointment in Denmark, has transmitted to us the following farewell lines to bis friends in this Island, which we with pleasure give publicity to : Suffering from ill health and a severe blow received during the hurricane on the 2nd of August 1837, I was prevented by my sudden departure on the 21th of May last year from personally paying my respects to many dear friends and acquaintances in the Island. Circumstances have induced me to wish to remain in Denmark, and an official appointment, now most graciously granted me by His Majesty the King, prevents my return to the Westindies. The remembrance of all the happy hours spent there during more then twenty years, all the kind services and politeness received from the inhabitants throng on my heart, and it is with deep feeling, that I bring my Inst Farewell to all in the beautiful island Ste. Croix the garden of the Westindies. Mav I have the satisfaction, that, as sure as 1 never intended to do harm to any one, and to be of service, where I con'd, 1 may be kindly remembered by all, and may health and prospeiitv attend on ail my triends left there. Copenhagen the 31 si May 1839. G. A. KOEFOED.

Excessive Politeness. þÿ Mr. Rowland Hill was alwavs annoyed when their happened to he any noise in the chapel, or when any thing occured to divert the attention of his hearers from what he was saying. (In one occasion, about three days before his death he was preaching to one of the most crowded congregations that ever assembled to bear him. In the middle of his discourse, he observed a great commotion in the gallery. For a time he took no notice of it, hut finding it increasing, he paused in his sermon, and looking in the direction in which the confusion prevailed, he exclaimed, " \V hat's the matter there ?" "The devil seems to have got among you !" A plain country looking man immedrately started to his leet and addressing Mr. Hill in reply, said, " No, Sir, it am't the Devil as is doing it ; it is a lady wot's fainted ; and she's a very fat un. Sir, as don't seem likely to come to again in a hurry" "Oh, that's it, is it !" observed " Mr. Ilill, drawing his hand across his cliin, then 1 beg the lady's pardon þÿ and the Devil's too."

The Eccaleobion. þÿ A curious exhibition, under the name of the " Ecualeobion," is about to be opened to-morrow in Pail mall. It is a machine heated by steam, and divided into various compartments foi the hatching of birds by artilicial heat. There is also another machine, in which eggs of every date, from the time of their being laid until 21 days old, are so placed, that by means of a strong artificial light they are rendered transparent, so that the spectator can observe the progress of the hatching, lrom the origin of litis in the chicken until us complete formation. þÿ One side of the large room in which the exhibition is placed is set apart for the chickens when hatched, and bears the appearance of a miniature poultry-yard. The contrivance is an improvement on the Egyptian mode of artilicial hatching in ovens, and is well worthy the visit of the naturaiist and the curious.

The Soft Place and a Scf/er one. þÿ The Duchess of Kingston, in her day, was licentious and eccentric. She once appeared at a highly fashionable ball in a flesh colour, d dress, which almost conveyed the semblance of nudity. King George II. was present, and attracted by the levity and accessibility of her bosom, at the same time whispering, "How delicious, how soft a place!" "Do you think so?" said the Duchess, "if your Majesty will concede me your hand. 1 will put it on a yet softer place." The King did so, and the Duchess laid it on Ins owu head.

New Food For Horses. þÿ At a period, when fodder is so extremely high, it is very desirable that a substitute should be found. þÿ It appears from the following, that Sago is likelv to be used in place of grain, and from the nourishing quality of that tood, we have every reason to suppose it will succeed. Sago is not manufactured in this Island, but we doubt not it can be imported at a cheap rate, and if it can be substituted for oats in Scotland at a saving of 25 per cent., there is is no reason why we should not encourage its introduction in large quantities into this Is land. Sago as Food for Horses. þÿ We lay before our readers a letter from a gentleman, whom we consider as of first rate authority þÿ one whose opinion is of some consequence either on the turf, or stable economy þÿ it is as follows, and we give it at full length : þÿ towards Edinburgh, Dece nber 2 8th, 1838. Mr Bail don. Sir þÿ In answer to your enquiries to me, as to the result of my feeding horses on Sago. I have not. until now felt at liberty to give it, noi chosing to do so until I was perfectly satisfied on the subject myself. " 1 have now, however, had a very fair trial of this food for nearly three months, and on a considerable number of horses. 1 have now, and have had for some time past, twentynine horses feeding with Sago, twice a day and thirteen horses feeding four times a day, or altogether on Sago ; that is to say, without any oats. 1 find that those horses stand their work as well, if not better, than when fed on

the best oats, and my saving cannot be estimated at less than 25 per cent, in favour of the Sago. I have out of this number of horses two which do not take it so well as the others, which are very fond of it. " I conceive Sago is peculiarly suitable as food for hunters, in the proportion of one pound of Sago to three gallons of water, will be found, 1 should think, a most valuable restorative to hunters after a severe day in the field The best way to make this, is to take a quantity of the Sago prepared in the ordinary way, and dilute it with warm water to the necessary extent, or, if the Sago is more conveniently carried by the groom dry, one pound can be softened with five ounces of affectionate and well ordered family. boiling water, arid then diluted with the necessary quantity of water. " 1 am satisfied, that if Sago can be supplied in sufficient quantity to be sold at the present moderate price that it must always rank high as an article of food for horses. " You are at liberty to make what use you please of this letter. " I am, Sir, your obedient Servant. " Isaac Scott." We may just add that Air. Baildon, 73, Prince's Street, has this day published some valuable information, "on the use of Sago for feeding horses, dogs, cows, pigs, and poultry." þÿ Edinburgh Paper.

FAMILY GOVERNMENT. Columns of newspapers and volumes of honks have been written on this subject, and to very good purpose in many cases. But alter ail, the secret is more in a nut-shell than is commonly supposed The greatest secret in the whole matter consists in being a truly good parent. Your children see you in your domestic, carelessness. They know the real character of their parents better than persons

If they find their parents unkind to each other, or failing in any way to maintain in private the characters which they assume in public, their respect is gone, þÿ their confidence broken down If your child has ever known vou to be guilty ot telling a lie, how can you govern him ? If he sees you in public putting on the air and manner and claiming to be a Christian, while in his close watchings he sees that you are full of pride and vanity and bitter feelings and ambition and covetousness ; that all your religion goes off at the corner of the streets, and none of it in your bedchamber ; how can you govern your child ? First, then, be a good man , and a good father. Secondly, govern, yourself, always, and without the least decree of unfair charity yourself The laws you enact for your children, never break yourself. If you break out with bad passion and excuse yourself, you must certainly be as generous to your children, and excuse them for the same fault in the same way. How can you govern yourself? Thirdly, let all your requirements be just and generous ; never given for your own good, but always for the good of your children. f ourthly, spare no pains þÿ give yourself no rest in body or mind, while any thing remains to be done winch can enlighten the understandings or sweeten the ufiections of your children. Fifthly, let your orders be wisely given, and then maintained at all hazards and all times. Never in one instance allow your

word to tail. Trust chiefly to kindness and persuasion and reasoning, and use punishment of any sort as little as possible. But let it be always understood that obedience full and entire, must be yielded to your directions. and that you will, though with great consideraleness and afiection, never slacken your hand nor relax your demands until such obediences is rendered. Mind these rules, and with very little severity in any way, you will seldom fail of securing all the benefits of a reciprocally

It is curious to compare the ideas entertained on this subject by two men the most opposite in nature þÿ the one a poet and sensualist, the other a stern moralist and philosopher. Lord Byron thus finely pictures the beau ideal of love ; þÿ " (Hi Love, no inhabitant o( earth tbou art !j An unseen seraph, we believe in thee ! A faith, whose mart) rs are (lie broken heart But never eye hath seen, nor ne'er shall see, The uuimagined form as il should be. The mind hath made thee, as it peoples heaven, Even with its own desiring phantasy : And lo a thought such shape and substance given, As haunts the iinquench'd soul, varied, wrung, and riven." I)r Johnson, more intelligibly and practically, thus speaks on the subject: þÿ "Those that have loved longest love best. A sudden blaze of kindness may, by a single blast of coldness, be extinguished ; but that fondness, winch length of time has connected with many

circumstances and occasions, though it may for a while be suppressed by disgust or resentment, with or without a cause, is hourly revived by accidental recollection. To those that have lived long together, every thing heard, and every tiling seen, recalls some pleasure communicated, or some benefit conferred þÿ some petty quarrel, or some friendly endearment.

Tradition ExTRAORDiNARY.--There is now living in the vicinity of Aberdeen, a gentleman who can boast personal acquaintance with an individual who had seen and conversed wilh another who had actually been present at the battle of Flodden Field. Marvellous as this may appear, it is not the less true. The gentleman to whom we allude was personally acquainted wi:h the celebrated Peter Garden, of Auchterless, who died in 1775, at the reputdd age of 131, although there is reason to believe that he was several years oloer. Peter, in his younger days, was servant to Garden of Troup, whom he accompanied on a journey through the north of England, where he saw and conversed with the famous Henry Jenkins, who died in lt>70, at the age of 1011 Jenkins was born in 1501, and was of course twelve years of age at the battle of Flodden Field ; and on that memorable occasion he bore arrows to an English nobleman whom he served in the capacity of page. Our reason for thinking that Peter Garden was older than be is reported to have been is this : There are still living individuals who knew Peter, and to whom he used to boast that he had served under Montrose, and been present at the fight of Fyvie. He used to say he was then a "gay loun," and page to Ogilvie of Foiglen. He had a vivid recollection of the encounter, and of the personal appearance of Montrose. The battle of Fyvie was fought in the tear 1044 ; and, supposing that Peter was then between ten and twelve years of age, he must have been at least 141 years old when

The English Ministkiis. þÿ If it were not so degrading e? rj to human nature, there would be something irrcistihly ludicrous in the cotnlimits of the London journals upon t lie recent failure of Sir Robert I'eel to establish himself and his political h iends in the seat ol power, inlluenue and profit, in England. The rancor of expression, and the extravagance of imputation, exhibited bv both parties, are not to be surpassed by any thing ever seen even in the most violent of our papers: and the abusive epithets heaped by the journalists upon each other would almost put to shame the " great Globe itself", or the most scurrilous of its party followers. We do not intend to dish up for our readers a catalogue of the ugly things averred or insinuated in relation to this matter by the Goliahs of the London press; but the prominent accusation on either side is worthy of notice, as affording an illustration of the party tone and spirit. The roarings of the Tory press are of course the loudest and most furious þÿ being elicitated by feelings of rage, disappointment and mortification. They affirm that the resignation o of the Whig o ministers was nothing but a paltry and disgraceful trick þÿ that the disagreement about the ladies of the Queen's household was all arranged beforehand þÿ and that the Queen, throughout the whole affair, was simply the dupe, or the willing tool, of Lords Melbourne and John Russel. The absurdity of these charges is so apparent that only men in a great passion could

be excused for making them. To say nothing ol the little likelihood that gentlemen of distinguished character would descend to a measure so despicable, the imputation upon the young and guileless Queen is to preposterous to be thought of. But even if this were not the case, the facts are demonstrative against the charge. How could the Whig ministers possibly know that Sir Robert Peel would insist upon dismissing the Queen's ladies, and resign if his demand was not granted? Or, to go still farther back in the inquiry, what possible motive could they have in resigning, with the intention of coming into olfiee again immediately ? How could thev know, even, that the Queen would resist Sir Robert's demand ? They cannot be supposed to have had this knowwas aware of, and a party to, ledge, unless it is assumed that ' the Queen the trick" ; and this idea is refuted, as well by her character as by the express declarations of Sir Robert Peel and the Duke of Wellington, that her conduct throughout the whole affair was marked by the utmost propriety and candor. The truth of the matter is, as we conceive, that Sir Robert overlooked one consideration which ought to have presented itself to his mind before any other. That the Queen would look upon his demand for the dismissal of her ladies as an intimation of his fears that she would suffer herself to be improperly influenced by them þÿ that they would intrigue against his interests, and that she would be either a party to, or the dupe of, their in-

trigues. C> This intimation she would naturally and justifiably consider an insult to herself; and resent and resist it accordingly. So much for the Tories. The givings-out of the Whigs arc not more generous or reasonable, although not uttered with so much acrimony and scurrility. They pretend to bchuvc that a most horrible design lurked , tonnage, 3,099. Ibid.

300333 &T33w under the demand of Sir Robert, for authority to sm round the Queen with ladies of his own choosing. They allude darkly to the heir presumptive þÿ (the Duke of Cumberland now King of Hanover) þÿ and the favor in which lie stands with the Tories ; they enlarge upon the Tory triumph that would be achieved bv his accession ; and with a wellfeigned shudder of alarm suggest the peril to which the Queen's life might be exposed, were the palace occupied by ladies of the Tory connexion. þÿ Upon the absurdity of such suggestions there is no need to comment. But there is one consideration growing out of this, and other aflaiis of similar nature, and of the comments thereon in the English journals, which is of some value to the people of tiiis country. It is well known that the bitterest enemies and revilers of our institutions, and the loudest proclaimcrs of the vast superiority which they ascribe to the monarchical form of government, are the English Tories. But it is the same 7'ories who complain so vehemently of the Queen's proceedings on the 8th and 9th of May ; who prophecy all manner of evil to England from the restoration of the Whig ministry ; and are so noisy and ferocious in their denunciations of the events that have caused that restoration. Now then, does R not follow that there must be radical and fatal defects in political institutions which afford opportunity t"i such events? Can monarchy be a form ol government so very superior and desirable, when it enables a girl of

twenty to defeat the patriotic designs and efforts of statesmen so illustrious as Sir Robert Peel and the Duke of Wellington unquestionable are, and so indispensable to the welfare of their country as their partizans proclaim them? þÿ These partizans atlirm that a large majority of the English people are Tory in feeling and in principle, and would rejoice to sec the government in the hands of a Tory ministry. If this is true is not the monarchy an evil, which enables an inexperienced young woman to keep out that ministry, and to retain in power men whose rule is so dolefully decalred to be nothing loss than ruin?

SINGULAR DREAM and DISAPPOINT- MENT. A curious incident lately occurred in our immediate neighbourhood. A gentleman who has a villa near tins, dreamt that a certain number would be a prize m the lottery. The morning alter his dream, which was a week previous to the drawing of the lottery, lie wrote a note to his clerk, to desire him to buy the ticRet immediately ; and subsequently told many of Ins neighbours and acquaintances of his dream, the number, and ol his purchase of tiie ticket. Being a very popular person, all who heard of the circumstance were anxious that his dream should be realized ; and, to their great satisfaction, the number was drawn a very large prize. þÿ forthwith, a numerous party of artisans and peasants employed by the gentleman in question, sailied forth from Naples, with musical instruments, colours flying, and a banner gaily decorated, on which the lucky number was insciibed, and also the amount of the prize, in this manner they proceeded to the habitation of Mr. , and announced the joylul intelligence, which, it is needless to say, spread a general hilarity through the house. This procession was followed by several friends and acquaintances, who came to congratulate the fortunate owner of the prize þÿ Refreshments in abundance were served out on the lawn for the peasants ami partisans, and a collation in the sail -a manger was oliercd to the friends, fcuffieient wine of an interior quality not being in the cellar, the best was supplied, in generosity the occasioned by the good fortune of the host. The

health o! the winner of the prize was repeatedly drunk, and many successions relative to the disposal of a portion of Lite newly acquired wealth were given. The news spread, and the pleasure grounds of Mr. became literally tilled with visitors of all classes ; when, in the midst of the general rejoicings, the clerk, who had been a week before deputed to purchase the ticket, arrived, with a visage so rueful and woe-begone, that one glance of it announced some disagreeable news. Alas! this unlucky wight had, in the pressure of more than ordinary business, forgotten lo buy the ticket ! and thought not of it until informed of its having been drawn a prize. The rage and disappointment of Mr. may be more easily imagined than described, when he saw the wheel of fortune, which had paused at his door, driven to thai of another ; who having heard of the dream of Mr. , selected the number, and became the buyer of the ticket only the day before it was drawn. The refreshments so liberally dispensed on this occasion had quite exhausted the larder of the dreamer, and nearly emptied his cellar ; and thus ended the affair of the lottery. Never were people so abdicated to this species of gambling as are the Neapolitans. All classes indulge in it more or less, but the lower ones give way to it with an extraordinary recklessness. Every dream, encounter incident, or accident, has

its own particular sign and number, which may be found in a book published for the instruction of the buyers of tickets, of which every house has a copy. The death ol a friend, however lameuled, refers to a particular number, which the mourner forgets not to secure, if it comes in conjunction with some fortunate sign. Thus even out of misfortunes and allliciions the Neapolitans seek to draw some recompense. Nor does frequent disappointment seem to correct their eagerness tor the lottery. þÿ They always discover some satisfactory reason lor having missed the prize, and hope to be more fortunate the next time. þÿ The Idler in Italy, by Lady Blessington.

Thediscoveries astronomers have made are truly subjects of admiration. This immense globe on which we live, has moved uniformly ever since creation, at the rate of 18 miles in a second, which is more than a thousand miles in a minute, or 51 ti, 000, 000 miles in a year. Ot course, since Lite creation it has moved about tour millions of millions of miles --a distance as far as beyond the strongest concepiions of the mind as infinitely itself; and yet this immense distance is but one eighth of the distance ot the nearest fixed stars; which is thirty two millions of millions ot miles þÿ a distance so great that a cannon ball, flying at its usual rate would be nearly a million of years in reaching it. T he sun, together with the planets, revolving around it seem to excite the idea of a family of kindred worlds. Their greatness, their distance, their beauty, the harmony of their motions, are objects vastly sublime. þÿ Yet all Ihe solar system when compared with the constellations of fixed stars, are no more than a drop of water compared with the ocean. We judge of every thing by comparison þÿ Nothing is absolutely great or small that we can comprehend. The planet Mercury is very near the sun. According to the temperament of our earth, it must be hot. While llerschcll, the planet last discovered, by reason of its immense distance must be extremely cold. But Venus, the morning and evening star, being but a little nearer the sun than we are, must be of a delightful temperature,

1 often gaze with pleasing wonder on this beautiful planet. It is larger than our earth It must have a greater portion of light. It is placed in a mild region of the system and is probably the seat of bliss.

Increase of The Growth of Cotto.v In the year 1791 the amount of cotton exported from the United States was 188.316 lbs ; in 1798 it was not quite 1,900,000 lbs. ; in 1802 it was 27,501 ,075 lbs. ; in 1819 it was 87,997,045 lbs.; in 1820 it was 127,860,152 lbs ; in 1830 it was 898,459,102 lbs. The amount exported in 1838 was upward of 639,000,000 lbs. ; leaving for home consumption 08,000,000 lbs. ; the whole crop in round numbers, being estimated at seven hundred and thirty-seven millions of pounds, which, at fourteen cents per pound, would be worth more than one hundred millions of dollars. This is a greater amount than ever was produced from all the gold and silver mines in the whole world in one year.

From tkr. Jamaica Morning Journal, July 10. ANOTHER SLAVEIl. H. M. Brig Snake has captured another slaver, bound to Cuba with a human cargo. The Snake sailed lVoin Halifax on the 23d last month, for (his place. On the 31 inst. she fell iii with, 01T the Island of l'orto Rico, and captured the Spanish schooner Carridad de Cuba, from the coast of Africa out 27 days bound to St J ago de Cuba, vvitli one hundred and seventy one slaves on hoard. The small pox had broken out on board tiiis vessel, and there were ten persons afflicted with that disease. Both the Snake and her prize have been placed under quarantine, and will sail for the Havanuah on Wednesday morning.

another slaver captured. The following account of the capture of another slave ship is taken from the Montego Bay Standard of the 17th July : þÿ "On the morning of the 4th ult H. M. schooner Pickle observed a very suspicious look tig vessel standing in for the height of Pines, to which she immediately gave chase firing several guns for the purpose of bringing her to; but to which the stiariger paid no attention, continuing to run directly for the laud un h-r a heavy press of canvass, and soon alter commenned heaving overboard casks and other articles to lighten her. " The Pickle, gaining fast on her, now fired several shots witii grape and oannister, which fell thick around her ; but such was the determined obstinacy of the crew that it was perceived they laid flat on the deck on every gun being (ired, and jumped up immediately after, and ran forward in her bows in order to bring her on an even keel, to enable her to ground nearer the shore. "After the chase of six hours, the vessel, which had hoisted Portuguese colours, ran on shore in the bight, distant about two cables length, when Lieut. Holland dispatched his boats to capture her. It was now seen that the crew were pitching the negroes into the sea, an I, on the boats Hearing, they jumped overboard themselves, swam to the shore, and escaped into tiie thick mangrove bushes on the water's edge, On taking possession of the vessel, she proved to he the schooner iSicrra del Pilar, 78 days from Onim, from the African coast, with 180 negroes on board

several of whom were in a most emaciated condition. She had originally 255, but death and several who had escaped into the woods with the ciew, had reduced the number to 180. The scene of misery and filth which now presented itself on board this vessel is inconceivable, and on getting her afloat, she leaked so much, and had such a small quantity of fresh water on board, that Lieut. Holland. nlicr being at sea some days, deemed it advisable, for the preservation ol the lives of the prize crew and negroes, to tran ship them on board the Pickle, and destroy the Sierra del Pilar, which was accordingly done oil' Gape Antonio on the 8th, the water then being on the water casks up the slave deck ; and her trim being so bad, as to have greatly endangered Iter foundering the previous night in several very heavy squalls. " From having such an addition to her complement, the Pickle steered for the Havaima, the nearest port, where she arrived on the 12th ; and lrom papers found on board

the Sierra del Pilar, which proved her to be bona fide Spanish property, was condemned there by the Court ot Mixed Commission, and the negroes transhipped to H. M. ship Rornney, in the charge of Dr. R. R. Madden, the Superintendant of liberated Africans.'! þÿ Ibid July 19.

EXTRAORDINARY CASE OF MONO- MANIA. Some 30 years ago a young lady, the only daughter of a noble house in the north of Germany, from having been one of the most cheerful girls became subject to fits of the deepest melancholy. All the entreaties of her parents were insufficient to draw from her the reason of it ; to their affection she was cold, to their caresses rude, and. though society failed to enliven her she bore her part in it with a power and venom of sarcasm that were as strange to her former character as they were unbecoming her sex and youth. The parents contrived, during her temporary absence from home, to investigate the contents of her writing-desk, but no indications O 7 of a concealed or disappointed passion were to be found, and it was equally clear that no papers has been removed. The first news they heard of her was, that the house in which she was visiting had been burnt to the ground; that she had been saved with difficulty, though her room was not in that part of the building where the lire had commenced ; that her escape had at first been taken tor granted, and that when her door was burst open she was found still dressed and seated in her usual melancholy attitude, with her eyes fixed on the ground. She returned home neither altered in manner nor changed in demeanour, and as painfully brilliant in conversation when forced into it. Within two months of her return the house was burnt to the ground, and her mother perished in the flames; she was again found in the same stale as on the former occasion, sullered her-

self to be led away without eagerness or resistance, did not alter her deportment upon hearing the fate of her mother, made no attempt to console her father and replied to the condolence of her friends with a bitterness and scorn almost demoniacal. The father and daughter removed to a spa for change of scene. On the night of their arrival the hotel was in flames ; but this time the fire began in her apartment, for from her window were the sparks first seen to issue, and again was she found dressed, seated, and in a reverie. The hotel was the property of the sovereign of the little state in which the spa was situated. An investigation look place ; she was arrested, and at once confessed that on each of the three occasions she had been the culprit ; that she could not tell wherefore, exctqrt that she had an irresistablo longing © © to set houses on fire. Eacii time she had striven against it as long as she could, but was unable to withstand the temptation ; that this longing tiist supervened a lew weeks after she hud been seized with a sudden depiessiou of spirits: that she felt a hatred to all the world, but had strength to refrain from oaths ami curses against it. She is at this moment in a madhouse, where she was at first allowed some liberty, but after an exhibition of homicidal monomania towards a child, of a ferocity most appalling, it was found necessary toapply the severest restraint. She still possesses Iter memory, her reason-
ing power, her petulant wit, and obacrve® the most scrupulous delicacy. þÿ Monthly Jju» Magazine.

Wiiat would Dr. Johnson þÿsay? We published amongst our miscellaneous serai, on Wednesday, an extract from the London Quarterly, in which it is indirectly had what would fir Johnson have said, if he asked been told, sixty years ago, that the tiny volume of steam, issuing from the spoilt of his black iron tea kettle, was a power competent to rebuke the waves, and set even the hurricane at defiance. The learned Doctor has himself answered the question of the learned reviewer in an article in the Ad- " venturer," of October 10: 1753: " Men unaccustomed to reason and researches, think every enterprise impracticable, which is extended beyond common effects, or comprises many intermediate opperations. would consider a flight through the air in Many that presume to laugh at projectors, a winged chariot, and the movement ot a mighty engine bv the steam of water, as equally the dream of mechanic lunacy ; and would hear with equal negligence, of the onset of Thames and Severn by a canal, and the scheme of Albuquerque, the Viceroy of the Indies who in the rage of hostility bad contrived to make Egypt a barren desert, by turning the Nile into the Red Sea." The Thames and severn are united by a canal, and the movement of a mighty engine bv the steam of water, is no longer a novelty. It is said, bv the Newark Adverlizer, " Let men take a iesson from their amazement at the past and present, and cease to prophesy against the future. The fly on the coach wheel who thought he kicked up the dust,
was a modest philosopher, compared with the man who ventures to read the future and prescribe limits to the advances ot science. Hie Barbadian.

Sir Nicholas Bacon, a judge in the time of Queen Elizabeth, was once, while on the bench, importuned by a criminal to spare his life on account ot his kindred. How so 1 asked the judge. Because my name is Hog, and yours is Bacon, and hog and bacon is so near akin that they cannot be separated þÿ " Aye," said the judge, " hut you and I cannot be kindred until you be hanged, for hog is not bacon until it is well hanged.

THE LOVE OF A VIRTUOUS WIFE. By Li mm LEnclns. Were I a man and had the fortune to win a heart, with what parsimony would 1 use my advantage ! How many gradations would I oblige myself to pass thro' suecessively and slowly ! How many delicate pleasures, unknown to the generality of men, would 1, as it were, create to myself! Like the miser, 1 would incessantly contemplate mv treasure ; rejoice in the richness of it ; be conscious that it constituted my highest facility ; place my w hole scheme ot happiness in the possession of it ; in looking upon it as my own peculiar property, in being the absolute disposer of it ; and strengthen myself in the resolution not to lessen it by use. What transports to lead in the eyes of a lovely woman the dominion you have over her; to observe in all her actions relative to you, a still increasing tenderness ; to perceive her voice assume a softer tone, whenever she speaks to you; to view her blushes, even upon a compliment of course; and to triumph in her confusion upon any particular dress ! Can there he a situation on earth more flattering than that ofa lover, conscious of a reciprocoal flame ? And what surer proof can be required than instances like these ? How charming I to he expected with an impatience that her whole prudence cannot conceal : to be received with a welcome which charms the more by the endeavors which she makes, in part, to hide her transport ! ISlie has dressed herself to suit your taste; takes the very- meiri, the ascent, the whole air of a person that is known to he

most agreeable to you. Before, she used to adorn herself to charm your sex in general ; at present her toilet is spread lor you alone ; for you these jewels, this riband, that bracelet are put on ; you are the sole object of her whole attire ; you are become her second self, she loves you over again in her owu linage

A Virginia Barbecue þÿ A friend, who is a native of Virginia, his furnished us with the following account of the manner of arranging a barbecue at the South. An agreeable and retired place is selected, near some spring and pleasant grove. On the previous day, some favorite negroman of reputation for skill and experience in the business, is sent up with his assistants, who proceed to make a sort of kiln or pit of stories. Hogs of middling size, having due proportion of fat and lean, are then selected, dressed, and put to roasting, and constantly watched and turn cd during the night, and until they are ready, on the next day noon. They are sopped or basted with a sort of preparation of vinegar, peppers, and other spicy condiments, everv moment during the cooking, until the attack. When the proper time arrives (and every esiateJ gentleman prides himself on telling at a glance whether the thing is done right, " with just enough of the brown,") the animals are laid whole upon boards, and the company assembled round to feast. It then becomes the duty of every gentleman to feed the Indies , that is, to carve out those fat, spicy, rich and delicious morsels from the right places, and with ready tact. Nothing else eatable accompanies the hogs, except plain bread, with a few bottles of liquor fur those wh<> like it. These occasions are not usually large, but quiet and social, somewhat like a Massachusetts pic uic party, and commonly given in

turns by the owners of plantations. Sometimes the cost is previously estimated, and an assessment is made upon each gentleman for the amount. This is generally J the ar- O rangement when the party is large, andgived for political purposes, hy the friends ofa candidate for office. The feasting over, if the weather be fine, singing claims attention, or the company adjourn to the neighboring house for a dance, leaving the remains of the entertainment for the negroes, who, in their turn, feed, rejoice, and make merry. þÿ Bangor Whig.

There is a class, now greatly multiplying in this country, and generally overlooked by politicians in their calculations þÿ those men of talent and instruction who are just below the rank in society which would of itself entitle them to associate with gentlemen" Persons of this class have tlie activity and energy, which higher classes in our state civilization and education almost universally want. They have hitherto exerted that activity in other spheres. It is but of yesterday that they have begun to read and to think. They have now many oftheadvunj 'ages for mental cultivation which were so long confined to tbe higher classes þÿ and they are using them. There are more hard stuby tbe Hastings family, and must lend to 1 dents, more vigorous seekers of knowledge, in this class, than there are at present in any other, and out of all proportion more who study the art of turning their knowledge to practical ends. They are, as it is natural they should be Radicals to a man, and Radi cals generally of a deep shade. þÿ They are the natural enemies of an order of things in which they are not in their proper place- We could name seveiul men of this class, of whom it is as certain as any prediction in human allairs can be, that they will emerge nto light and make a figure in the world. TK1U VTPH3 OF AMERICAN MECHANICS. Mr. Nonius, of Philadelphia, promises to obtain for himselt and country an enviable reputation. The locomotive made by order for the Birmingham and Gloucester rail road, England, has arrived out to its destination, and succeeded to admiration þÿ performing the conditions required, vi. twenty miles an hour, in much less than the time. The most flattering encomiums are expressed of it in the English papers. It weighs only eight tons, and drew a load of one hundred and twenty. Its engine is stated to be of a simplicity, neatness aud finish of workmanship, quite surpassing any thing of the kind in England, outstripping their locomotives in speed, though these last were heavier. The boiler also has but 70 instead ol a hundred tubes, like the English. The whole machinery is more compact ; and such is the mathematical precision, says the English account, that the steam joints are constructed merely by the co-aptation of polished metallic surfaces, needing no packing. The company in Falkland are so delighted with tins locomotive, named þÿ The England," that sight more are ordered. IO3 Thus has the time arrived that our mechanics are taking a position for workmanship, as well as ingenuity of invention. Necessity is the mother of invention. We have thousands of miles more rail road than any other country, therefore it stands to reason our locomotives are more perfected. For the same reason, as nearly all the steam navigation in England is on the sea, their steam ships surpass ours. But great capitalists in

our sea ports should look to the above facts in proof of the assertion reiterated in the Star that our mechanics can make also, if they put out their strength, a steam ship in its model, machinery, &o. equal probably, in every respect, to the beau ideal of naval perfection now booming over the Atlantic to this port þÿ we mean the British Queen. þÿ iV. We have received intelligence from a quarter that can he relied on, of the intentions of Mexico towards Texas. The Mexican troops are to approach the western confines ol Texas in small detachments simultaneously and to rendezvous on the Rio Brazos, until the grand body shall number about 8000 men. The centre is to be supported by a detachment of cavalry, stretched to the right and left, so as to sweep the whole country. The invading force is not to be less than 12,00 ) men. þÿ An exterminating war is to be waged. þÿ No quarters, to man, woman, or child, will be the watchword. Not a house to be left standing in the country. Universal pillage is to be allowed to incite the soldiery to action The whole command is to devolve upon Bustamente, and should he he worsted in his march by the Texians, Santa Anna is to take the field in person, at the head of 10,000 men The campaign is to begin in September. þÿ N. O. True American.

PARIS, June 24. STATE OF PARIS. I am sorry to state that in consequence of the various discoveries lately made by the police, it has become necessary to secure even the chimneys of the Palace of the Tuilerics, by iron bars across both within and without, to prevent those who meditated entering the Pulice by the chimneys, and assassinating the King and Royal Family, from carrying their object into effect. It has also been deemed expedient to erect within the Palace a sort of observatory, from which all that passes outside the Palace may be at the same moment received and reported. Still, though this measure will answer the proposed object in the day time, it can be of no use at night. The only effectual scheme will be to fortify the 'Pufferies, and not leave it, as it is at present, an open palace The police also enforces with great rigour the execution of the ordonnance relative to þÿgunsmiths shops ; and in spite of the protests made to the contrary, no guns are allowed to be kept in hand at those establishments in a state fit for immediate use.

PROPOSED TERRITORIAL ARRANGEMENTS OF PRUSSIA WITH HOLLAND. Private letters from the Hague of a very recent date lead me to believe that there is a serious project of a territorial arrangement between Prussia and Holland, arising out of the late settlement ol the Hutch Belgian question by the treaty of the 24 Articles Prussia will cede the country of Cleves to Holland, and will receive in return the German portion of Luxembourg detached from Belgium by the treaty in question. The King of Holland is the Grand Duke of Luxembourg, but the town and fort which give the title to the province is a federal fortress, where civil authority is wholly annulled by military authority. The King of Holland will transform Maestricht into a federal fortress, if he can obtain the town of Treves to make the seat of a duchy as a substitute for that of Luxembourg. This arrangement would suit the German Confederation. By the possession Maestricht, the German Confederation would be mistress of both banks of the Lower Meuse, and could act as it thought fit against France or her neighbours. Of course France will cry out furiously against this arrangement' as the dominion of Prussia in Luxembourg would be most annoying to France.

DAYS LATER This splendid steam ship arrived Sunday morning about 10 o'clock, in less than sixieei days, having left Portsmouth on the 12th iii.;tnrit, at 12 o'clock, P. M. She made the Floating Light, Sunday morning, 1 o'clock, and soon after the Highlands and Sandy Hook, and waited awhile for a Pilot. The wind was general against her all the passage, and sometimes very rough þÿ but large as she is, one man could steer her. She proved throughout the first rate sailer. The number of her Passengers is 127, among whom is Mr. Junius Smith, to whom is awarded the honor of first starting in England the idea of Ocean Steam Navigation Companies. The arrival of the Big Ship, as she fired off her guns, then making a sweep in the North River, announced her own approach, created a great sensation in the city, and immense crowds followed her to the place of stopping, þÿ the new Piers of the Tobacco Warehouse, which has been especially fitted up, and with gates, for the reception of the Steatn Ships The crowds continued all day, and thousands and thousands wore eager to have a view. þÿ It is understood, however, that as efforts will be made to get her off August 1st, it will þÿ not be possible to see company till the next vovage. o As the British Queen and the Great Western are now side by side, occupying the inside berths of their two new Piers, the contrast is a great curiosity, and well worth a visit to observe. The Great Western was a wonder, þÿ but the contrast sinks her into a

common steamer. The top of her funnel is but barely visible over the deck of the Queen, as an observer stands on her pier. Both ships stand how to bow, their figure head projecting over the main land, and their wheel houses almost touching, þÿ but the Queen tills out the Pier, and stretches her bowsprit a considerable distance upon the land Her prodigious bulk is the amazement ot all who sue her. Her puddle wheels, now her coal is consumed, are nearly out of water, and she looms up, like an observatory in the air. It is thought, that to make her sit sufficiently deep the water, in she must take in a good deal of ballast, þÿ for her paddle wheels have not, during the voyage, dipped deeply enough to throw her ahead with a velocity proportioned to her model and her power. Her model is American. Among the Passengers in the Queen are Colonel Mudge and Mr. Fealherslonaugh, who are commissioned to make a scientific reconnoissance of the Boundary Line between Maine and New Brunswick. They act independently, and for the British Government alone. It is not all remarkable that the appointment of Mr. Featherstonaugh should create remark in America, for we understood hint to be, or to have been, " Geologist to the United States," þÿ but we now presume no such officer ever existed. The money market continued in the same state as hv the last advices. The Bank of England had not advanced the rate of interest beyond 5 J per cent. This, with the fact of ar, increase of the revenue for the last quar-
ter, affected money matters somewhat favourably. The crops in England are said to be promising, and in some parts the harvest had already commenced.

Lord Palmerson stated that an application bad been made to the Government in the early part of last year by persons from Texas, for the purpose of knowing whether the Government were preparing to acknowledge the in" dependence ot Texas.
