Butler, in a speech in Parliament on a late occasion, said þÿ Whenever I contemplate the condition of the working classes the deep and dark gull þÿ that separates them from the knowledge and sympathies of their superiors in fortune, the utter ignorance<iri which we are of their feelings and wonts, the little influence which we have over their conduct, and the little hold which we appear to have on their affections þÿ 1 shrink with terror from the wild passions and dense ignorance that appear to be fermenting in that mass of physical for e. We see vast portions of them utterly neglected, utterly uniustructed, and plunged in debauchery, during the intervals of toil. Among another and yet wider class, we may observe the spread of thought yet more pernicious' and the intercommunication of sympathies vet more menacing Sometimes the murmur of their discontent and ignorance assumes an articulate form, and speaks in the accents of the disciples ot Thorn, the followers of Stephens, and the millions whose creed is Chartism ; for such are the instructors to whom you leave the minds of the people. Some learn their religion from a I nana tic, in whose resurrection they believe; others are taught that every man has a right to what wages lie thinks reasonable, and that he may ertforce his right by the dagger and the torch. learn that rents and profits are a deduction from wages, and consequently believe that the owners of land and capital are the plunderers and oppressors of the workman. þÿ These doctrines advance unencountered by the morality or the simple political reason which would dispel their influence. As had been anticipated, orders have been given to release the Canadian prisoners in England, on their entering into personal securities not to return to Canada. Lady Flora Hastings. þÿ The remains of this lady were conveyed from London to Leith in a steamboat, July 5. From Edinburgh they will be conveyed to Loudoun Castle, the seat of her maternal ancestors, a distance of sixty miles. Lady H. was Lady of the Bedchamber to the Duchess of þÿKent. She was accused a short time since of being enciente. and the household physician declared the charge to be correct, and hence the difficulty that has arisen. On a post mortem examination ol the deceased lady's person the physicians expressly declared that the most ordinary and necessary functions of the liuman tramc " must have been interrupted and interfered with," from causes "that could only be referred to some former and distant period of time." So that except a life of incessant suffering were desirable, Lady F'lora Hasting's death is a mercy, Not only, therefore, is it certified, under the hands of five eminent medical authorities, that the cause of death was wholly unconnected with a disturbed stale of mind, or what is familiarly called a "broken heart," but that the said cause of death is referable to " some former and distant period of time" þÿ some time long prior to the period of the calamitous mistake that was in point of fact engendered by the very appearances which the disease assumed. She was 33 years of age,

K at Exterminator. þÿ The dangerous eonsequences frequently resulting from attempting to destroy rats with arsenic, has led to experiments lor the attainment of the end, by less hazardous means. The experiments have resulted in the following recommendation þÿ Reduce Plaster of Paris ( sulphate of lime) fine powder, mix it well with an equal to quantity of oat or irulian meal, and place it in the cellar, or other place infested with rats, and they will soon disappear. ANTKJU.Y. From the Weekly Register September 24. . We find that the Barque Euterpe from London which arrived here on Tuesday last the 17th, was nearly lost in a severe storm ori the 8th September not very distant from this Island. The following extract from the Log of the Ship was readily lent to us. The hours from 8 o'clock in the morning to six in the evening (land reckoning) are marked " Hurricane" There was nothing remarkable Jn the weather here at the time, altho' towards the close of August there were frequent indications ol bad weather. Barque Eutekpr from London toward Antigua, James IYIorrice Battinr, Commander . Remarks on SUNDAY 8th Sept. 1839. Commenced with strong breezes and passing showers of rain having all sail set low and aloft and steering about W. by S. | S. I.at. at noon 20' 30 N. and Long by account 18' 30 W. Long, by Chronometer. 40' 55 W. at 5 r. m. the breeze freshning and showers more frequent. In all studding sails Royals and topgallant sails, Blowing a gale. In close reefed topsails and furled the courses. At 8 p. >i. a complete Hurricane coming in violent gusts and the ship laving on her beam ends and laboring very heavy in tiie sea which was running in a manner that beats description, the crew trying the pumps but making very little water. Between 9 p. m. and midnight the Vessel was completely dismasted, having the tore and main top gallant masts cut away by the cap, Hying jib boom and sail, the gig was washed away and all our small sails shattered to pieces, the cook apparatus in the lee, scuppers and a number

of articles a missing. Midnight it still blew harder, the sea at times was more like a lake of fire than any thing it could be compared to. All hands on deck and all hatches battened down and the long boat double lashed, at day light abating a little, but the sea running violently, the head knees are all washed away and part of the starboard bulwarks, all hands clearing away the wreck. W e saw an interesting experiment this forenoon on board the revenue cutter Hamilton, Capt. Siurgis, which was intended to illustrate the practicability of raising a vessel by means ol cylindrical bags, placed under her bottom and filled wth atmospheric air. The bags were each ol large size capable of containing 2500 cubic feet of air. They were confined by means of ropes passing under the keel þÿ and afterward tilled by two forcing pumps, propelling the air through tubes into the cylindrical floats. The bags were made of three parts of stout cotton canvass, made air and water tight by means of India rubber arid were piepared by Mr. Howard of Boxbury, under the direction of the inventor, Mr. Mc'Kean. The cutter was raised considerably by the þÿprocess but the floats were made for a larger vessel, and when inflated, a large portion of them rose above the water. lhe utility of this þÿapparatus thus adopting a well known principle in pncumalicks to practical use, must be obvious to evcrv one.
It wiil enable vessels with large draughts of water to pass over barred harbors, as New

The Ice Mountain and the Hanging Rocks. While we were travelling, last summer' we passed through Hampshire county, in Virginia, and upon our return gave some no" tice of that remarkable mountain, and had the peculiar gratification of being laughed at for our pains þÿ Some good, and more poor jokes and puns, were perpetrated at the expence o ourself, and our newly discovered land. We have, however, patiently waited, and at length we find in a late number of the National Intelligencer a notice of Kercheval's History of the Valley of Virginia, and containing the following extract from it. "The Table Ice mountain, which Mr. K. thinks ' the most extraordinary and wonderful work of God's creation, and deserves the highest rank in the history of the natural curiosiiies of our country.' It is washed on one side by the Capon, and its west side, for about a mile, is covered with loose stones of various sizes, anil of diamond shape. It is from six hundred to seven hundred feet in height and on the western side for about one hundred yards, and ascending some thirty feet, when the loose stones are removed, the most perfect pure and crystal looking ice at all seasons of the year, is to be found in blocks of from one or two pounds to fifteen or twenty pounds weight.' " dzc. Not far distant from this mountain, there is to be seen on the South Branch, what is called the Hanging Rock, which seemed to us quite as remarkable as the Ice Mountain.

A very interesting experiment was mentioned by Raron Larrev, the favourite surgeon of Napoleon in one of the late sittings of the French Academy of Sciences During the campaign in Egypt this celebrated surgeou had observed that when the inhabitants of the country of the higher classes were labouring under confluent small-pox. which, there unmodified by vaccination, when it does not kill, leaves dreadful marks, the leeches of the country applied gold leaf over the whole surface of the body where the pustules had appeared. M Legrand, a French physician, on the suggestion of Rarou Larrey, employed this preservation in the case of a beautiful and young English lady of rank, labouring under one of the worst forms of this scourge. A coating of gold leaf, in the state in which it is employed for gilding, was applied to the face by the medium of a little gum to make it adhere. The young ladv recovered from the disease without marks except on the extremities and the central portions of the body where the gold leaf had not been applied.

From the Barbados Globe, Sept. 1 1». CONDITION OF THE ISLAND OF PORTO RICO.

The first thing that cannot fail to strike our West India friends is the composition of the population. þÿ Out of 357,003 souls, there were, in 1830, the lartje proportion of 188,000 or nearly 53 per cent, were slaves. The population thus composed is able to raise such an amount of produce, that after supplying all their own wants, the value of their exports exceeded in 1830, four million of dollars, including 25,000 tons of sugar, 3,000 tons of coffee, 1 ,700,000 galls, ofmolasses, 2,000,000 'hs cotton, and 5,500,000 lbs tobacco. It will be seen, from the tables, that with the exception to coflee, the quantities exported of the ditierent kinds of produce have been progressively increasing during the nine years to 18,10; and it is probable that the filling off in coflee may have been the result of unfavorable seasons. The average export of that article, in the nine years embraced by the table, was very nearly 0,000 tons per annum The total value of exports from the Island, so recently as 1803, was no more than 55,000 dollars, or oniy one-seventieth part of the value exported in 1830. The quantities of produce shipped in the former year were þÿ sugar, 71 tons; coffee. 131 tons: tobacco 108,000 lbs; cotton 102.000 lbs: with a few hides and spars. To what cause is the astonishing progress here mentioned to be ascribed ? For more than two centuries, Porto Rico li.nl been used as a place of banishment tor criminals from Spain ; the island was without trade, and its productions con-

sisted wholly of the commonest kinds of provisions, which were raised only in quantities necessary for the support of the inhabitants, who were too poor to indulge in artificial wants. 'I he civil and military establishments which were necessarily large, in consequence of the nature of a part of the population, were supported at a great expense to the mother-country ; and this state of things continued until 1815, when a royal decree was issued " for promoting the population, commerce, industry, and agriculture of the Island." Under this decree every encouragement was given to emigration of foreigners, to whom .lands were granted in proportion to the capital thev brought þÿ they and their descendants being guaranteed all the privileges of native Spaniards, in their full extent. The colonists were exempted from the payment of all internal taxes; the payment of tithes was suspended for fifteen years, and fixed after that time at one- fortieth only of the produce. These concessions wouid iiave been of little practical advantage, however, but for the privilege that was superadded, of free-trade with all parts of the world. I lie ports of the Island are opened to the ships of every power in amity with Spain ; and the planters are not limited in the sale of their produce ; hut may ship it to any market they may chose. At the same time, a system of municipal government was established throughout the colony, giving to every free person a voice in the appointment of those by whom the affairs of the town or

district in which he resides are engaged. The revenue, raised by means of import and export duties, is greater than is required for the government ol the colony, and a considerable surplus is every year icniitted to Spain.

I&AITSX T33!faWl>33X ;KB&33:#:tW»3 A/T33. This result, so different from anything , witnessed with respect to our West India Colonies, is not. however, the most remarkable point of dissimilarity. Free people and slaves are to be seen working together on the sugar plantations ; and not merely free people, but white people, labour in the canefields ; and under these circumstances, experience by natural causes a continual and great increase in their numbers. A good deal has lately been said about the necessity of introducing additional labourers into our Sugar Colonies. The local governments, in some of them, have offered great inducements to draw such to their shores, and much dissatisfaction has been expressed by our pi anters at the obstacles that have been opposed against the importation of Coolies from India. Why should not our English planters profit bv the example set them in Porto Rico? It might not answer to convey emigrants from this kingdom for the purpose. The natives of northern Europe might and probably would, prove unequal to the performance of field-labour in a tropical climate; but why should not the attempt be made to obtain the services of the poorer class ol white persons from the neighbouring conþÿtinents, thereby saving a great part of the expense and risk attendant upon so long a voyage as that from India, and securing a class of labourers accustomed to the climate, and whose bodily powers and energies arc far greater than are possessed by any of the natives of Hindustan. The introduction of any

number, however small, of labourers into Jamaica, at this moment might have a most powerful effect in bringing about a good understanding w ith the negroes, and establishing a fair rate of wages throughout. We shall at all times be thankful for any informations or suggestions, which persons possessed of local knowledge upon the subject, may be inclined to send us.

This magnificent vessel, the largest manof-war in the world, was launched from Pembroke Dockyard a few days ago Her dimensions areas follows: þÿ Length 225 feet beam between paddles 38 feet, depth of hold 21 fe:t. Her tonnage is about 1,300 being, 200 tons larger than the Gorgon, launched from the same slip about eighteen months since. Her equipment, as a man-of-war, will be the same in all respects as a frigate, having a complete gun or main deck, as well as an upper or quarter deck. On the main deck she will carry eighteen long 36 pounders, and on the upper deck four 48 pounders, and two 36 pounders on swivels, carrying a ball of ten inches diameter, and sweeping round the horizon 240 degrees. The Cyclops, like the vessel referred to, will be commanded bv a Post Captain, these two being the only steamers taking frigates' lank. Her crew will consist of 210 men, 20 engineers and stokers, and a lieutenant's party of marines, who will have charge ol the guns, all of which move upon slides and fixed pivots, thereby taking a much wider range than the ordinary carriage can gLe. She will be schooner riggid, but her foremast will be of the same scantling and height as that of a 36 gun frigate. Her draught of water, with all on board, including six months' provisions, completely armed, and with twenty days' fuel, will be fifteen feet. This quantity of fuel (100 tons) will be carried in the engine

room, but there is space in the fore and aftcf holds for ten days' more coal, making in all sufficient fuel for a thirty days' run She has an orlop deck below the gun deck, of dimensions so magnificient that there is room to stow with comfort eight hundred troops and their officers, so that, taking her all and all, the Cyclops may be considered the most powerful vessel in her Majesty's service. The Cyclops has teen builj in six months, under the immediate inspection of Mr. Wm. Eyde, master builder of Pembroke yard, from drawings and plans prepared by his brother, Mr. John Eyde. the able assistant of Sir W- Svmonds, surveyor of the navy, upon whose principle, namely, the combining of the sailing and steaming properties, this vessel has been constructed. The Gorgan already mentioned, is also built upon the same plan, and so admirably has it succeeded, that when on the coast of Spain that vessel not only eclipsed all that competed with her while under the power of steam, but in a trial of 300 miles under canvass in a stiff breeze beat the celebrated Pantaloon, heretofore supposed to be the fastest man of war brig afloat. Since the Gorgon was built experience has dictated many improvements, and these have been introduced into the Cyclops. The Cyclops will be docked in Sheerness dockyard on the 30th instant, and, alter remaining there for a few days, will proceed to the manufactory of Messrs. Seaward at Millwall, Poplar, to receive her engines, which will be of 320 horse power on the principle

which, in the case of the Gorgon, has proved so successful, that the Lords of the Admiralty have given orders for five more pairs of engines upon the same plan for as many frigates. Half a dozen such steamers would do three times as much work as the same number of line of battle ships. Twelve years ago Lord Cochrane maintained that a few well-appointed steamers would suffice to keep in check opposing fleets in the Mediterranean, and, if we may judge from appearances, a short time only will elapse before the experiment is tried. The Gorgon is commissioned by Captain C. Henderson, K. C. ST. THOMAS, October 9, 1839. Sporting Intelligence. þÿ On Saturday the 5th instant, came off on Long Point Course, St. Croix, one of the best contested races that has ever been witnessed in the Danish Islands. The match was between Mr. C. Srcnns' Sorrel Ponv Lazarus, and Mr. Kortright's Sorrel Mare Lady Lightfoot. The first heat was severely contested and won by the Cru/.ian Pony owing to 28 lbs. extra weight carried by I.azarus. But on equalizing the weights in the second heat, the superiority of the latter was very marked and odds of two to one were readily to be obtained in his favor on the third heat, which he led- and won in gallant style. The Course was ;very respectably attended, and the excitement evinced on the issue of this con 'est between the Sister Islands was ex. ceedingly great among all classes. Great credit is due to David Fin ley, Esq.. as trainer of the winning horse.
Sir Charles Metcalfe, the new Governor ot Jamaica, arrived at that island on the 2-ird ult. in II. B. M. t rigate Curucoa ; and Sir Lionel Smith left on the 1st inst. in the Serpent for New York.

London August 23d. The political news is favorable to the Peace of the World. The affairs of the East are being ended amicably. Mehemei Ali must give up his ambition to the Five Great Powers. The crisis, over sea, we verily believe is over, and what news we are to have, we now feel quite confident will be better news than we have had. France is quiet. The King and his Ministry now move on in concord. The riots of the Chartists in England are about over. The revival of Trade, of which there is every prospect, will soon give them enough work to do, and leave them no leisure for political meetings. The astonishing movements in England upon Ocean Sttam Navigation merit our profound attention. What a revolution is to be wrought by the introduction of the line of Steam Ships spoken of today in an extract from a London paper ! Lord Palmerston stated in the House of Commons, in answer to Mr. Hume, that on the 281 h of last month a note had been presented to the Almistcrs of the Porte, signed by the representatives of the Five Gicat Powers, technically called "a collective note, which stated that tlicy were instructed by their respective Governments to inform the Porte that the I'ivc Powers were agreed generally as to the affairs now pending between I urkey and Lgypt, and that they were directed to ask the Porte to suspend anv negotiations into which it might have entered with Mehemet Ali and not to proceed therein without the knowledge and concurrence of the Five Powers þÿ That note has been ac-

cepted by the 1 urkish Government with great thankfulness. The House might therefore be assured that there would he no disturbance of the peace of the East, unless some new subject of difference arose, of which there was no prospect whatever at present. Ibrahim, the conqueror, has halted in his career; Mehemet is negotiating with the Grand Seignior ; Russia is not making any

warlike preparations, and the English and French fleets are united at the mouth of the Dardanelles. Such is the substance of the last news arrived from the East. All this gives assurance for the peace of the world, and is sufficient to satisfy the claims of our national patriotism. France has contributed to the production of this state of things more than any other power. It was a French envoy who arrested the victorious march of Ibrahim and the French fleet was the first to arrive at Tenedos. þÿ Whatever may now be the direction taken by affairs in the East. France must be satisfied that she is worthily represented on the theatre of events. One of the King's sons has hastened to take part in the proceedings of her brave navy, and, come what will, we may be sure that we shall be prepared, as we have already been under circumstances equally unforeseen- We may wait with confidence the result of negoeiations supported by such antecedents þÿ Moniteur Parisian.

Our readers will be rejoiced to learn that Mr. Mc'Queen has at length, bv unremitted exertions, succeeded in establishing the long projected West Indian Steam Mail communication. All the great principles and details are settled with the Government, and so little remains now to be done, that there cannot possibly be any thing in the way of a speedy commencement of operations. The formation of the Company would have been publicly announced in London on the 13ih Aug. had it not been for the great pressure upon the Money Market, which is represented to be excessive. The Company will be called the "Royal Mail Steam Packet Company," having for its capital £1,500.000 in 15,000 shares of £l()0 each. More than half these shares, we learn, have been already bespoke. þÿ The company is established under a Royal Charter, and Government have contracted for the conveyance of the mails to the West Indies «fce., lor 10 years, at the rate of £210.000 per annum, to be paid in quarterly instalments. The leading Directors propose to place the general superintendence of the business of the Company in the hands of Mr. Mc'Queen, and it is therefore probable that gentleman will soon be among our Islands again, for ihe purpose of making arrangements with respect to the several Agencies Goal Depots, &c. Parties are extremely sanguine as to the success of the present magnificent undertaking and as it appears that Government will give all its influence and place the vessels ol the Company on the same footing as the

present packets, in order to free them from Custom house entries, Port Charges, &c. ifec. ; they may perhaps be justly so. For our own parts, we shall be glad to see it in successful and continued operation. Nothing can be more unsatisfactory than the arrangement with respect to the present packets þÿ

nothing more desirable than that what would tend to improve them. We have times out of number given publicity to complaints on the subject, and no longer than yesterday, we had io remark that the Mail had lain at St. Thomas's for six days before a Steamer could be procured to bring it down here.- þÿ This calls for a remedy which we hope will tie speedily applied. þÿ Jamaica Morning Journal, September 27.

Teelatalism. þÿ Professor Edgar, of 'Belfast, an active member of the British and Foreign Temperance Society, has published a letter against tee-totalism. The work is dedicated to the Bishop of London, president of the British and Foreign Temperance Society, the first great principle of which is abstinence from distilled spirits, and moderation in the use of other liquors. The professor denounces (he tee-totallers as men who would inflict a privation on society, which is no where commanded in the Scripture. He adds, that by following out the arguments of the teetotallers, our Saviour himself, who drank wine, and used it as the symbol of his blood, would be convicted of a flagrant impropriety. The professor, who is Doctor of Divinity in Belfast College, lias rio objection that men who cannot drink ale without getting drunk should he tee totallers ; hut then, he says, he should not, like the fox without the tail, endeavor to bring down to the same brutal level those who have been in the habit of wisely making wine and ale a moderate part of their diet. St. Paul prescribed wine to Timothy, not as medicine, but as part of diet. The Sciiptures generally have wine and meat as a matter ol indifference ; hut the tee totallers abstain from w ine, and then exalt their conduct into a superscriptural virtue. The learned professor then argues that, as the teetotallers insist upon total abstinence ironr wine because some drink too much of it, so they ought also to preach entire abstinence

fiom meat, because some eat too much flesh ; indeed, he savs, they would contend for the latter privation more rigorously, because, lor one man who lias died in an excess from wine, a thousand will he found to have killed themselves from the "gormandizing, stuffing, stimulating, and repletion" that our fellow subjects are unfortunately, too generally inclined to practise in the eating line. Fanaticism oi evcrv species is sure eventually to defeat its own object, and there is every reason to believe that tee totallers have brought even temperance into ridicule through their vehement and loolish, however well meant, zeal in pushing their impracticable doctrines to the extremes they have done. þÿ London paper.

Hints In Business Men. þÿ Superintend in person as much of your business as practicable, and observe with a watchful eye the management of what is necessarily committed to the agency of others Beware of sell indulgence ; no business can possibly thrive under the shade of its influence. Never lose sight of the powerful influence of example, and be careful in the management of your concerns, to recommend by your own personal practice uniform habits of active, interested, persevering diligence to those in your employ. Despatch at once, possible, if whatever you may take in hand ; if interrupted by some unavoidable interference, resume and finish it as soon as the obstruction is removed. Do not assume to yourself more credit for what you do than you arc entitled to, rather be content with a little less þÿ the public will always discover where merit is due. Familiarise yourself with your hooks ; keep accurately and frequently investigate and adjust their contents. This is an important item. Avoid display. Wear your learning like your watch, in a private pocket, and don't pull it out to show that you have one ; but if you are asked what o'clock it is, lull it.

The Lord Chancellor, on his knee presented the speech to the Queen, w hich her Majesty read, as follows, in her usual distinct and impressive manner; þÿ ' My Lords <$ Gentlemen, " The public business having been brnughi to a close I have now to perform the satisfactory duty of releasing you iiom vouriong and laborious attendance in parliament. " 1 rejoice that a definite treaty between Holland and Helgium, negociated by the me-
diation of the Five Powers has settled the difference between these two canities, and has secured the peace of Europe from dangers to which il hud so lung been expose J.

" The same concord which brought these intricate questions to a peaceful termination prevails with regard to the a (lairs of the Levant. The Five Powers are alike determined to uphold the independence and integrity of the Ottoman empire, and I trust that this union will ensure a satisfactory settlement of matters which are of the deepest importance to lite whole of Europe. " It has afforded me the sincerest pleasure to have been able to assist in effecting a reconciliation between France and Mexico þÿ Intent upon preserving for mv subjects the blessings peace, of I am highly gratified when I can avail myself of an opportunity of removing misunderstandings between other Powers. " I have recently concluded with the King of the French a convention calculated to put an end to differences which have arisen of late years between the fishermen of Great Britain and of France. This convention, by removing causes of dispute, will tend to cement that union between the two countries which is so advantageous to both, and so conducive to the general interests of Europe. " 1 shall continue to pursue with perseverance the negociations in which 1 am engaged, to persuade all the powers of Christendom to unite in a general league for the entire extinction of the slavetrade, and I trust that, with the blessing of Providence, mv efforts in so righteous a cause will he rewarded with success. "I regret that the differences which led to the withdrawal of mv ministers from the court of Tehran have not vet been satisfacto-

rily adjusted by the government of Persia. " lu order to fulfil the engagements announced to you at the opening of ihe present session, the Governor General of India has moved an armv across the Indus, and 1 have much satisfaction in being able to inform you that the advance of that expedition lias been hitherto unopposed, and there is everv reason to hope that the important objects, for which these military operations have been undertaken, will he finally obtained. ' I have observed with much approbation the attention which you have bestowed upon the internal state and condition of the country. I entirely concur m the measures which you have framed for the preservation of order, the repression of crime, and the better administration of justice in this metropolis, and I have given a cordial assent to the bills which you have presented to me for the establishment of a more efficient constabulary force in those towns which peculiarly required it. and for effecting the important object of generally extending and invigorating the civil power throughout the country. " Gentlemen of the House o f Commons, " I tnank you tor the goal and readiness with which yon have voted the supplies for the serv ice ol the year. " It lia» been with satisfaction that I have given my assent to a reduction of the postage duties. 1 trust that the act which has passed on this subject will he a relief and encouragetnent to trade, and that hv facilitating intercourse and correspondence it will he produc-

tive of much social advantage and improvement. I have given directions that the preliminary step should be taken to give effect to the intention of parliament, as soon as the inquiries and arrangements required for this purpose shall have been completed " The advantageous terms upon which a considerable amount of the Unfunded Debt has been converted into Stock, .'afford a satisfactory proofed the reliance placed on the

baiter vszyrmmziL »a<MKB2xr<os ATIS. credit and resources of the country, as well as on your determination to preserve inviolate the national faith. " My Lords and Gentlemen, l'lt is with great pain that 1 found myself compelled to enforce the law against those who no longer concealed their design of resisting hv force the lawful authorities, and of subverting the institutions of the country. þÿ The solemn proceedings of courts of justice, and the fearless administration of the law by all who are engaged in that duty, have cheeked the first attempts at insubordination; and I rely securely upon the good sense of my people, and upon their attachment to the constitution, for the maintenance of law and order, which are as necessary for the protection of the poor as for the welfare of the wealthier classes of the community." The Great Western steamer cast anchor in Kingroad Bristol, yesterday morning, at half-past rive þÿo clock, after a remarkably fine rapid voyage from New York of 12 days and a half. She brings 04 passengers. The most interesting news she firings is the intelligence of her own triumph in point of speed over her formidable competitor, the British Queen. On the 3d instant the smoke of the British Queen was lost sight of by the Great Western, and she was not seeu subsequently during the voyage.

PARIS, Aug 3. NEWS FROM TUB BAST. The French government has received the following telegraphic dispatch : þÿ Alexandria, July 16. ' THE CONSUI, GENERAL TO THE PUESCUENT OF TIIE COUNCIL. The Turkish fleet came here on the 14th, under the command of the Capitan Pacha, to place itself at the disposition of .Vlehemet Ali. The Viceroy said he would not restore it to the Porte until the Grand Vizier Khosrew Pacha should be dismissed from office, and the crown of the countries governed bv him (the Viceroy) should be declared hereditary. The Egyptian army has received orders to retire on the Syrian side of the Euphrates." PARIS, Aug 12. A letter from Alexandria of July 15 says, « The English government has transmitted a note to the Pacha, calling upon him to give an explicit declaration ot Si i s motives in sending troops to the Persian Guit ; wishing to ascertain whether these troops are destined to take possession of Basora. The Egyptian government has replied that it would be an absurdity to imagine that these troops were intended for Bassora, or even Bagdad, as the Pacha had never entertained any such idea, and that his only object was to chase the pirates who infest these seas, and do great injury to the commerce of Europe as well as to that of Arabia. Nevertheless, to give prool of his pacific dispositions, Mcheinet Ali has promised that he will immediately send orders to Kurschid Pacha to evacuate the Bahrim þÿislands. The Gazette þÿ1 iedmontese of the 8th instant slates, under date Trieste, 3d instant, that the

Gapilan Pacha delivered into the hands of Mcheinet Ali 22 vessels of the Ottoman fleet, which had altogether consisted of 34 þÿsail. þÿ The commanders of three ships of the line, and of nine frigates and smaller vessels, refused to follow him, and had been met sailing back to Constantinople. The last accounts from llonmelia received in Constantinople were dated Rumkaieh, where Hatiz Pacha had established his head-quarters. Ibralmn Pacha was still at Aleppo on the 7th. Captain Cullicr (aide-de-camp of Marshal Soult) bad an interview with him on the 4th, The news from the East given in the German papers appears to require confirmation, Thus the Augsburgh Guzette of the 8lh inst.. states, under date Alexandria, ltiih ult., that on the proceeding evening the consuls of the Great Powers wailed on Mehetiiel Ail, and

JDARSXL T23TI1T1i23E ttatgEOlSTOS formally demanded of him to send hack the Ottoman fleet to Constantinople, The Pacha replied to them. þÿ The fleet does not belong to me; it is the property of the Sultan, as well as my fleet, my army, and all the countries under my domination Therefore, whether the Ottoman fleet be at Alexandria or at Constantinople, it is still within the territory ot the Sultan, who may dispose of it as he pleases. If he wishes it to return to Constantinople. let him sav so, and 1 will proceed mvself thither if he desires me." The consuls had nothing to reply to such a declaration, and merely reported what had passed at the interview to their respective governments.

PARIS, Aug. 13. THE EASTERN QUESTION. The Debuts says þÿ þÿ A proposition has been made to our Cabinet by the English government, that the United English & French fleets should proceed to demand the forcible restoration of ttie Ottoman fleet. As this fleet would certainly refuse to surrender, and wouid be assisted by the Egyptian fleet, what has been proposed was nothing short of a second Navarino. England would have hud tiie satislaelion of destroying both the Egyptian and the Turkish fleets : but the English fleet, it was generously offered forsooth, would defend the entrance of the Bosphorous against Russia. On occasion of the ninth anniversary of the accession of Louis Philippe to the throne, his Majesty has been graciously pleased to grant pardons, commutations, or diminutions of punishment to 719 persons condemned to

Origin of þÿ þÿFoolscap Paper þÿ It is well known tfiat Charles I. of England, granted numerous monopolies for the support ol his government. Among others was the privjlege of manufacturing paper. Th W'aler -' mark of the finest sort was the royal arms of England. The consumption of this article was great, at this time, and large fortunes were made by those who had purchased the exclusive right to vend it. This, among other monopolies, was set aside by the Parliament that brought Charles to the scaffold, and by way of showing their contempt for the King, they ordered the royal arms to be taken from the paper, and a fool, with his cap and bells, to be substituted. It is now more than an hundred and seventy-five years since the þÿfool cap s and bells were taken from the
paper, but still, paper of the size which the Rump Parliament ordered for |their journals, bears the name of the water mark then ordered as an indignity to Charles.

The Sea Serpent once more ! þÿ If more proof were wanting of the existence of the Sea Serpent, and of his presence in our waters at this time, we have it in the annexed extract from the last Kennebunk Gazette: þÿ He was seen last week ofT the Nubble, near Cape Neddiek, by the crews of seveial boats, one of which came in close contact with his majesty. This boat was manned by two seamen of þÿ long þÿstanding, þÿ with one of whom we are acquainted, and know him to be a man of unquestionable varacity, good judgement, and that his statements are deserving of entire credit. He informs, that while pulling from Cape Neddiek harbor, in a small boat, in the afternoon of the 13th, when about a mile and a half from the harbor, he saw, about 30 feet from the boat, a school of sharks as he supposed at first sight, but he was convinced after a þÿmoment s observation, that it was the huge marine monster so frequently alluded to as the Sea Serpent. He thinks the boat passed over a part of him, ns only a part of him was visible when first noticed. He afterwards saw him distinctly. His length, he says, cannot he short of 100 feet þÿ has bunches or bumps on his back, about the size of a common barrel, with flippers at each end of them þÿ is covered with scales the size of a common plate þÿ has a small head, resembling somewhat that of a þÿsnake -passes through the water with extreme velocity, and his motions resemble those of a snake. He was in the vicinity ol the boats for some time, dodging about, probably, in

search of food, and finally set ofl for the eastward. Several of the þÿboats crews were much alarmed and made tor the land. Our informant thinks he could not have been deceived --he has seen shoals of various kinds of fish ; he lias seen whales, sharks &c. &c. but this resembled no marine animal þÿ or cluster of marine animals, which he has ever before met with. We give the statement very nearly in the words of our inþÿformant.

The Sea Serpent was seen off Nahant on Sunday evening, by a large number of ladies and gentlemen, lie made his appearance about six þÿo clock, and continued in sight about three quarters of an hour. At one time he was near the rocks, and his movements could be distinctly seen.

The efforts of tiie poor to ohtain an honest livelihood. þÿ The various means adopted by poor people (particularly widows with large families) to gain an honest livelihood, are passed over by the great mass of the community with indifference ; yet they are nevertheless highly commendable and praiseworthy. The persevering efforts of some of these poor creatures is really astonishing Rendered destitute as they are by the death of their husbands, it is surprising to see the manv little schemes they project, to acquire an honorable, and, in some measure, an independent subsistence Let us not turn then with a contemptuous sneer from the picture of human beings, however mean and poor, exerting their skill in honest, though often ineffectual, endeavors to support their families ; there is a blessing on industry, even if exerted in the most trifling degree. How respectable it seems in comparison with idleness and pampered vice! I low noble are the eflorts of till such unaided individuals ! and how much are these eflorts calculated to produce happy reflections, in comparison with the exertions of the dissolute in squandering the means of others, or (bat listless indolence which induces reliance upon the exertions of others for a support ! The poor industrious widow is a respectable member of society, compared with the dissolute spendthrift, or the lazy idle loafer who are equally objects of reproach and contempt. Mow gratifying it is, when the endeavors of the poor people are crown-

ed w'itli success ; how blessed it is, not only as regards themselves and (heir little families, but as respects the welfare of the whole community. We should admire the utility of such excellent examples, and never turn with affected contempt from the efforts of the industrious poor. Rather let us learn to sympathise in their fate, as beings fully as good, but not as lucky as ourselves, and in the spectacle of enduring hope which they often present, be mor and more impressed with the conviction that Tt evidence never refuses to yield protection and consolation to the afilieted, nor leaves the desolole to mourn. þÿ New York Sun.

washing, and a saving of labor. The recipes for making have been sold from 5 to $10, and the soap 7 cents per pound ; but can he manufactured for about two cents. Take two pounds of sal soda, two pounds of y el low bar soap, and ten quarts of water ; cut the soap in thin slices, and boil all together two hours ; then strain it through a cloth ; let it cool, and it is fit for use. Directions for using the soap: þÿ Put the clothes in soak the night before you wash, and to every pail of water in which you boil them, add one pound of soap They will need no rubbing ; merely rinse them out, and they will be perfectly clean and white.

Changes of the Universe. þÿ Every thing around us is in a constant state of motion, yet nothing falls into disorder. The heavenly bodies perform their revolutions with the utmost possible regularity. Even those eccentric I bodies, comets, have their orbits, and travel rejrularlv within tlieir allotted space, How ! regularly and invariably do the seasons depart and return ! Spring and Summer, seed time and harvest, never fail to return. The visible world itself is perpetually .undergoing changes. The earth is constantly -being deprived of its nourishing juices by the plants and roots. But is it, therefore, worn out and rendered sterile? No; for the same Being who has ordained that the vegetable and the animal creation shall depend upon the þÿearth s fecundity for support, has ordained, likewise, that that fecundity shall he perpetually renev « ed and maintained. With our own frames it is the same. At every instant of our lives we arc literally wearing out our bodies. Insensible perspiration alone deprives us, every day, of some pounds weight of our substance. But the aliments which God has provided for us replace the waste thus caused, and restore us the strength we expend. How wonderful is the wisdom which has thus provided for the continued existence of the universe! how wonderful, also, is the power which has, from the beginning of time, instituted this unvarying succession of circumstances ! Can we reflect upon the innumerable manifestations of this power and of
this wisdom without feeling the highest admiration and the utmost humility? Above all, when we icflect upon the innumerable instance in which, to tins power and this vvis-

dom, there is added a boundless and almost incredible benevolence, can we fail to be penetrated by the most sincere and profound gratitude. If we meditate aright we must surely cannot : let us, then, not become guilty, as well as unwise, by neglecting thus to meditate.
